sections.h2: Where is Washington County, Nebraska, and what is in it?
sections.html:
Washington County is a small county in eastern Nebraska, just north of Douglas County and the Omaha area, with Blair as its county seat. It was created on November 23, 1854, named for George Washington, and was one of the eight original counties proclaimed by acting Governor Thomas B. Cuming.

Washington County factDetail
County seatBlair
Total area393.2 square miles, about 390 of it land
2020 census population20,865
CitiesBlair, Fort Calhoun
VillagesArlington, Herman, Kennard, Washington
Neighboring countiesBurt, Douglas and Dodge in Nebraska; Harrison and Pottawattamie in Iowa
HighwaysU.S. 30 and 75; Nebraska 31, 91 and 133

Most of the county is farmland, with the small towns above scattered across it. Fontanelle is a census-designated place, and De Soto, Nashville, Orum, Spiker and Telbasta are unincorporated communities. A homeowner here may be in a town, in a village or on a rural parcel, and that choice decides which municipal rules apply on top of the county's.

sections.h2: What is the story of Blair, the county seat?
sections.html:
Blair was platted in 1869 when the Sioux City and Pacific Railroad extended to the site, and it took its name from the railroad magnate John Insley Blair. The town incorporated as a city in 1872 and became the county seat within its first year.

The city sits in the Loess Hills with the Missouri River valley around it, and it belongs to the Omaha and Council Bluffs metro area. The 2020 census counted 7,790 residents. Blair was home to Dana College from 1884 until the school closed in 2010. The Missouri River floods of 2011 reached the Blair bridge area, which is a reminder that low ground near the river carries flood risk.

sections.h2: What drives the Washington County economy?
sections.html:
Agriculture covers much of the land, while Blair adds distribution and other employers. Economic development for the city and the county is handled jointly by the City of Blair and Gateway Development Corporation, the county-wide development group, which works from 1646 Washington Street in Blair. Blair also runs a local economic development program authorized under Nebraska's Local Option Municipal Economic Development Act, known as LB840.

The best-documented recent project is a Dollar General distribution center. The state economic development department announced in November 2020 that the company planned a ground-up center in Blair combining about 650,000 square feet of dry goods space and about 150,000 square feet for fresh items, with 400 new jobs at full capacity and completion slated for 2022. A large employer like this changes demand for houses in Blair and nearby villages, because workers look for homes within commuting distance.

sections.h2: Which county offices handle property tax in Washington County?
sections.html:
Four offices matter to a property owner, and each does a different job. The Assessor values property, the Clerk takes valuation protests for the Board of Equalization, the Treasurer collects the tax, and the Register of Deeds records the transfer.

sections.h2: How does Nebraska value a Washington County home?
sections.html:
Nebraska assesses property as of January 1 each year, and the state standard for residential property is at or near 100 percent of actual value. The county's protest page repeats that houses, rural homes, buildings, commercial and industrial property, recreational property and mobile homes are held to 100 percent of market, while agricultural land is held to 75 percent of market and is valued using soil maps and land use such as dry, irrigated or grassland.

The tax itself is the taxable value multiplied by the consolidated rate for the tax district, expressed per $100 of value. A house inside a town bills county, municipal and school district levies together, so two houses with the same value can have different bills if they sit in different districts.

The county assessor sends a notice by June 1 to the owner of record as of May 20 for any parcel whose value changed. Homestead exemption applications, which can exempt all or part of a home's value for qualifying owners, are filed with the assessor between February 1 and June 30.

sections.h2: How do you protest or appeal a valuation in Washington County?
sections.html:
You can protest real property value by filing Form 422 with the County Clerk on or before June 30, and the county asks owners to talk to the Assessor's staff first, because that conversation may make a protest unnecessary. The steps are short.

  1. Talk to the Assessor's office about how the value was set.
  2. File Form 422 with the Clerk by June 30, stating the value you request, the basis for it and the legal description. A protest that does not give reasons can be dismissed.
  3. Ask for a review by the Assessor's office if you want one. A referee who is a registered appraiser may meet with you before the Board of Equalization hearing.
  4. Attend the hearing. The Clerk tells you the time and place and notifies you of the Board's decision within seven days of the final action.
  5. If you disagree, appeal to the Tax Equalization and Review Commission within 30 days after the Board adjourns. For protests handled in the June 1 to July 25 session, adjournment is deemed July 25.

The county notes that a protest covers valuation only and is not a challenge to the tax rate. For houses, comparable sales or a recent appraisal are the usual evidence. Personal property protests are due earlier, by May 1.

sections.h2: When is Washington County property tax due, and what happens if it is late?
sections.html:
Real and personal property taxes are due December 31, the first half becomes delinquent the following May 1 and the second half on September 1. Nebraska law sets interest on delinquent taxes owed to political subdivisions at 14 percent a year.

Payments can be mailed to the Washington County Treasurer, P.O. Box 348, Blair, NE 68008, or made online through the county's payment vendor. For personal property, the county states that on the due date the tax becomes a first lien on all personal property you own, and taxable or not, that property can be seized to satisfy it.

This calendar differs from the one in neighboring Douglas County, where the first half is delinquent April 1 and the second August 1, so owners who moved from Omaha into the county should reset their reminders.

Unpaid real estate tax can lead to a county tax sale. Nebraska Revised Statute 77-1801 sets the collection of delinquent real property taxes by sale in relation to the first Monday of March, and Statute 77-1802 requires the county treasurer to prepare a list of the delinquent real property four to six weeks before that Monday. If you own a house with back taxes, getting a payoff figure early gives you the most choices, whether that is paying, selling or negotiating a sale.

sections.h2: What does it cost to record a deed and sell a house with tax due?
sections.html:
A sale in Washington County is recorded by the Register of Deeds, which charges a $10 first-page fee and $6 for each added page, with certified copies at $1.50 a page. A Real Estate Transfer Statement, Form 521, must accompany the deed.

The Nebraska Department of Revenue lists the documentary stamp tax at $3.32 for each $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026, falling on the grantor. The county's own fee page still shows an older per-thousand figure, so rely on the state's current number. On a $225,000 sale, the state rate gives $747.

If taxes are owed at closing, they are normally paid from the sale proceeds through the title company, which also splits the current year's bill between the parties. Ask for the title company's statement before the signing date so no figure comes as a surprise. A house with delinquent taxes can still close, because the payoff usually comes out of the price.

faqs.q: When is the Washington County, Nebraska property tax protest deadline?
faqs.a: Real property protests must be filed with the County Clerk on or before June 30. Personal property protests are due by May 1. Use Form 422, state the value you want and explain why.

faqs.q: When do Washington County taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: The first half is delinquent after May 1 and the second half after September 1, following the December 31 due date. Interest is 14 percent a year under Nebraska law. You can pay by mail to P.O. Box 348 in Blair or online.

faqs.q: Can I sell my house in Washington County if I owe property tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Back taxes are normally paid from the proceeds at closing, and the title company confirms the payoff. Get a balance from the Treasurer, phone (402) 426-6888, before you sign anything.

faqs.q: Who do I call to dispute my Washington County property value?
faqs.a: Start with the County Assessor's office, then file Form 422 with the County Clerk at 1555 Colfax Street in Blair if the issue remains. The Clerk's number is (402) 426-6822.
